questions.prompt: A convex quadratic program allows only affine constraints. Which added constraint keeps the program convex?
options: \(x^2-y^2\le 1\), whose Hessian has a negative eigenvalue
\(-x^2-y^2\le -1\), the outside of the unit disk
\(xy\le 1\), with an indefinite Hessian
questions.explanation: A quadratic inequality \(g(x)\le 0\) describes a convex set when the Hessian of \(g\) is positive semidefinite. The disk is a sum of squares, so its Hessian is positive semidefinite. A negative eigenvalue, the outside of a disk, and the product \(xy\) all fail that test.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-6)^2\) subject to \(x^2\le 4\). What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The constraint is the interval \([-2,2]\). The parabola \((x-6)^2\) decreases as \(x\) increases toward 6, so the best feasible point is the right endpoint \(x=2\). The value is \((2-6)^2=16\). The number 6 is the unconstrained decision, and it is not feasible. The number 4 is the right-hand side of the constraint, not the objective value. The left endpoint \(x=-2\) gives \(({-2}-6)^2=64\), which is worse.

questions.prompt: The objective of a quadratic program is already convex, and its constraints are affine. You add one quadratic inequality. The new program stays convex when
options: the new left-hand side has a positive semidefinite Hessian
the new left-hand side has a negative eigenvalue
the new constraint is the outside of a disk
the new constraint uses a square, regardless of the sign of the Hessian
questions.explanation: Convexity of a sublevel set \(\{x:g(x)\le 0\}\) follows when \(g\) is a convex function. For a quadratic \(g\), that is the positive-semidefinite test on its Hessian. A negative eigenvalue makes \(g\) nonconvex. The outside of a disk is a superlevel set of a convex square, and it is not convex. Using a square is not enough: the sign of the Hessian matters.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that decides whether a program with quadratic inequalities is a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program. Each step uses the object the previous step named.
questions.explanation: The left-hand sides have to be written before their Hessians are the matrices being tested. Those Hessians have to be read before the positive-semidefinite test can accept or reject them. Acceptance has to come before a minimizer is called global. Swapping an adjacent pair tests a matrix or a status that has not been produced yet.
steps: Write every constraint with a quadratic function on the left of a less-than-or-equal sign.
Read the Hessian of the objective and the Hessian of each of those left-hand sides.
Accept the program as convex only when every one of those Hessians is positive semidefinite.
Treat a minimizer of an accepted program as a global minimizer.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-5)^2+(y-5)^2\) subject to \((x-2)^2+(y-1)^2\le 9\). The unconstrained point lies outside the disk. What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The feasible set is the disk of radius 3 centered at \((2,1)\). The point \((5,5)\) lies at distance \(\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\) from the center, so it is outside. The nearest feasible point is 2 units closer, on the segment from the center to \((5,5)\). The squared distance from \((5,5)\) to that point is \(2^2=4\). The radius 3 is not the objective value. The center is feasible and scores \((2-5)^2+(1-5)^2=25\), which is worse than 4.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-1)^2+(y-1)^2\) subject to \((x-4)^2+(y-5)^2\le 4\). The unconstrained point lies outside the disk. What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The disk has center \((4,5)\) and radius 2. The point \((1,1)\) is at distance 5 from the center, because the offset is \((-3,-4)\). The gap from the point to the disk is \(5-2=3\), and the squared gap is 9. The squared distance all the way to the center is 25, which scores the center, not the boundary point that the objective prefers. The radius 2 is the constraint, not the objective value.

questions.prompt: Let \(c>m+\sqrt{s}\) with \(s>0\). Minimize \((x-c)^2\) subject to \((x-m)^2\le s\). Write the optimal value in \(c\), \(m\), and \(s\).
questions.explanation:
The constraint is the interval centered at \(m\) with radius \(\sqrt{s}\). Because \(c\) lies to the right of that interval, the best feasible point is the right endpoint \(m+\sqrt{s}\). The optimal value is the square of the gap from \(c\) to that endpoint.
• \((c-m)^2\) forgets the radius.
• \((c-m-s)^2\) subtracts \(s\) instead of its square root.
• \(c-m-\sqrt{s}\) is the gap, not the objective value.

questions.prompt: The inequality \(x^2-4y\le 0\) is the set where \(y\) sits above a square. Its Hessian in \((x,y)\) is diagonal with entries 2 and 0. This constraint is
options: not convex, because one diagonal entry is zero
not convex, because a square is curved
convex, because both diagonal entries are nonnegative
a half-space, because the boundary is a straight line
questions.explanation: The left-hand side \(x^2-4y\) has Hessian \(\mathrm{diag}(2,0)\), which is positive semidefinite, so the sublevel set is convex. A zero eigenvalue does not spoil that test. The boundary is a parabola, not a straight line, but a curved boundary can still enclose a convex set. The epigraph of a convex function is the picture of that fact.

questions.prompt: Which inequalities are convex quadratic constraints?
options: \(xy\le 1\)
questions.explanation: The disk is a sum of squares, so its Hessian is positive semidefinite. The square of an affine function has a rank-one positive-semidefinite Hessian, and its sublevel set is a closed slab between two parallel lines. The inequality \(-x^2-y^2\le -1\) is the outside of the unit disk, and the Hessian is negative definite. The product \(xy\) has an indefinite Hessian, so its sublevel set is not convex.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The constraint under discussion is \(x^2\ge 4\).
questions.explanation: The set is the outside of an interval, and the chord test fails, so it is not convex. The rewritten left-hand side \(4-x^2\) has second derivative \(-2\), which means it is concave, not convex. A convex quadratic constraint needs the opposite curvature test. The false step swaps that sign.
steps: The set \(x^2\ge 4\) contains \(-3\) and \(3\) but not \(0\).
The chord from \(-3\) to \(3\) therefore leaves the set, so the set is not convex.
Writing the set as \(4-x^2\le 0\) produces a left-hand side whose second derivative is negative, and a negative second derivative means that left-hand side is convex.
A convex quadratic constraint would instead need a positive semidefinite Hessian on the left of a less-than-or-equal sign.
reasons: A negative second derivative means the left-hand side is concave, not convex.
The points -3 and 3 are not both feasible.
The chord from -3 to 3 stays inside the set.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-8)^2+y^2\) subject to \(x^2+y^2\le 9\). The unconstrained point lies outside the disk. What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The feasible set is the disk of radius 3 centered at the origin. The point \((8,0)\) is at distance 8 from the origin, so the gap to the disk is \(8-3=5\). The squared gap is 25. The nearest feasible point is \((3,0)\), and \((3-8)^2=25\). The squared distance to the origin is 64, which is the score of the center, not of the boundary point the objective prefers. The radius 3 is not the objective value.

questions.prompt: The disk \(\lVert(x,y)\rVert\le 3\) is a convex quadratic constraint. It is also the special case of a later form in which a Euclidean norm is bounded by an affine function. That later form is
options: an equality-constrained Newton step
a second-order-cone constraint, here with a constant upper bound
a semidefinite constraint on a nonsymmetric matrix
an absolute penalty added to a squared residual
questions.explanation: The inequality \(\lVert(x,y)\rVert\le 3\) already has a Euclidean norm on the left and an affine function, the constant 3, on the right. That is a second-order-cone constraint. A Newton step is an algorithm, not this constraint. A semidefinite constraint asks a symmetric matrix to be positive semidefinite. An absolute penalty is an objective term, not this disk.
